title: SR&ED Capital Expenditures - Canadian R&D Tax Glossary
description: Learn about the historical rules and current treatment of SR&ED Capital Expenditures in our Canadian R&D tax credit glossary.
summary: SR&ED capital expenditures are taxpayers' costs for depreciable property used all or substantially all (90 per cent or more of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. Ineligible from January 1, 2014, they are again claimable under the section 37 deduction and investment tax credit for property acquired, or lease amounts first payable, on or after December 16, 2024.

body.text: SR&ED capital expenditures are taxpayers' costs for depreciable property used all or substantially all (90 per cent or more of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. Ineligible from January 1, 2014, they are again claimable under the section 37 deduction and investment tax credit for property acquired, or lease amounts first payable, on or after December 16, 2024.
Executive Summary and Macroeconomic Architecture

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program stands as the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and development, supporting more than 22,000 claimants annually across the country, including approximately 4,000 corporations within the province of Québec alone. Administered jointly through policy formulation by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program operates through a dual-mechanism architecture embedded within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the "ITA"). First, the statutory framework allows taxpayers to pool and deduct eligible current and restored capital R&D expenditures against taxable income in the year incurred or carry them forward indefinitely. Second, the legislation awards an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a baseline rate of 15 per cent to an enhanced refundable rate of 35 per cent on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade. Prompted by persistent structural productivity gaps relative to peer Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) economies and concerns over domestic intellectual property (IP) retention, the Department of Finance launched a two-phase national consultation in early 2024. This comprehensive policy review culminated in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement (effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), which committed $1.9 billion over six years to expand the program's capital and scale-up parameters. Specifically, the federal government proposed to increase the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35 per cent ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million, elevate the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, extend the 35 per cent refundable credit to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restore the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs that had been repealed in 2014. Budget 2025, tabled on November 4, 2025, raised the proposed expenditure limit to $6 million, and the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted these measures for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Québec enacted a sweeping structural consolidation in its March 25, 2025 budget, eliminating five legacy R&D-related tax credits for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, to streamline provincial innovation support.

From a structural tax policy perspective, these federal and provincial reforms signal a deliberate pivot away from subsidizing solely early-stage micro-enterprises toward retaining mid-market scale-ups and capital-intensive domestic manufacturing. By previously restricting the 35 per cent refundable credit exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) with under $50 million in taxable capital and excluding capital equipment, the legacy regime inadvertently penalized domestic technology companies that accessed public equity markets or invested heavily in physical pilot plants and laboratory hardware. Extending refundability to eligible Canadian public corporations and restoring capital expenditure eligibility directly mitigates the liquidity disincentive associated with domestic public listings and capital-intensive commercialization, while the CRA simultaneously tightens administrative audit scrutiny over contemporaneous documentation and systematic experimentation.
Statutory and Legislative Framework
Core Provisions of the Federal Income Tax Act and Regulations

The legal authority governing federal R&D tax incentives is codified across primary intersections of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Understanding the statutory interplay among these provisions is essential for both claim preparation and audit defence, as an expenditure must satisfy sequential gates of technical definition, pool deductibility, and investment tax credit qualification.

Subsection 248(1) of the ITA establishes the substantive legal threshold for what constitutes eligible scientific research and experimental development across all Canadian tax provisions. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Within this statutory architecture, eligible work is categorized into three foundational research and development pillars alongside a strictly bounded category of directly supporting activities. Paragraph (a) of the definition encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (b) covers applied research, which comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (c) governs experimental development, representing the vast majority of industrial claims and encompassing work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Complementing these three core pillars, paragraph (d) admits work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly limits eligibility to circumstances where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude activities that, while commercially vital or technically complex, do not resolve underlying scientific or technological uncertainty through systematic experimentation. These statutory exclusions disallow market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

Once an activity satisfies the technical definition under subsection 248(1), Section 37 of the ITA governs the deductibility of expenditures incurred by a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada for SR&ED carried on in Canada under subsection 37(1). Rather than forcing taxpayers to capitalize R&D costs or deduct them strictly within the year incurred under general business income calculation rules, subsection 37(1) aggregates eligible current expenditures—and, for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, eligible capital expenditures—into a cumulative tax pool. Any undeducted balance in the subsection 37(1) pool may be carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable business income in subsequent taxation years. To prevent double-dipping between tax deductions and tax credits, paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(t) mandate that any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a taxation year (whether utilized to offset Part I tax or received as a cash refund) reduces the subsection 37(1) pool in the following taxation year, and where that reduction exceeds the remaining pool balance, the excess is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable income. Procedurally, subsection 37(11) establishes the strict statutory filing deadline for reporting expenditures on prescribed Form T661.

Parallel to the Section 37 deduction mechanism, Section 127 of the ITA governs the calculation and pool mechanics of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Subsection 127(5) permits a taxpayer to deduct earned ITCs from Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, while subsection 127(9) codifies the critical statutory definitions of "investment tax credit" (establishing the baseline 15 per cent credit rate alongside the 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback windows), "qualified expenditure," and "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool". Subsections 127(10.1) and 127(10.2) provide the additional 20 per cent ITC—bringing the total enhanced rate to 35 per cent—up to a qualifying corporation's annual expenditure limit. Furthermore, subsection 127(26) enforces anti-accrual discipline on unpaid amounts other than salaries or wages, deeming expenditures that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which they were incurred not to have been incurred until the taxation year in which they are actually paid. Where a qualifying corporation has no Part I tax payable or its earned ITCs exceed its federal tax liability, Section 127.1 of the ITA provides the statutory authority for the CRA to refund unused ITCs in cash. Finally, Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations prescribes the granular rules for eligible overhead expenditures under the Traditional Method (subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3)) and the calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method (subsections 2900(4) through 2900(10)), including the specific statutory caps placed on specified employees.
The 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Reforms and Modernization

On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance initiated a formal legislative consultation on modernizing the SR&ED program to better support R&D-intensive Canadian businesses and promote domestic IP retention. The first phase of these consultations examined how the SR&ED architecture could remain competitive, how eligibility definitions should evolve, and how the program could ensure that intellectual property funded by Canadian taxpayers remains anchored within Canadian-owned and operated enterprises. Phase one closed on April 15, 2024, immediately preceding the tabling of Federal Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance on April 16, 2024. Budget 2024 initially earmarked $600 million over four years commencing in 2025–26 ($750 million over five years, with $150 million per year ongoing) and launched a second phase of technical consultations that ran through May 27, 2024.

Following extensive stakeholder submissions during phase two, the Department of Finance substantially expanded its fiscal commitment in the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement (announced December 13–16, 2024), proposing $1.9 billion over six years to enact four structural reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. First, the federal government expanded the enhanced expenditure limit, proposing to increase the annual ceiling on qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the enhanced 35 per cent ITC rate by 50 per cent, from $3.0 million to $4.5 million. Budget 2025 raised the proposed ceiling to $6.0 million, and the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 enacted the $6.0 million expenditure limit for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. As a direct consequence, the maximum annual fully refundable federal cash credit for qualifying corporations rose from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Second, the reforms widened the taxable capital phase-out range. Previously, the $3.0 million expenditure limit began phasing out on a straight-line basis when an associated corporate group's taxable capital employed in Canada in the preceding taxation year reached $10 million, becoming completely eliminated at $50 million. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the phase-out floor and ceiling increased by 50 per cent to $15 million and $75 million, respectively, allowing capital-intensive mid-market corporations to retain access to the enhanced refundable rate as they scale.

Third, the December 2024 reforms extended eligibility for the enhanced 35 per cent refundable tax credit to eligible Canadian public corporations on up to $6 million of qualifying SR&ED expenditures annually (as enacted), with the expenditure limit phased out between $15 million and $75 million of average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years rather than by reference to taxable capital; a CCPC, or all CCPCs in one of the associated corporate groups, may elect to use the same revenue-based calculation under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the ITA. Historically, the 35 per cent refundable rate was restricted exclusively to CCPCs; if a Canadian technology or life sciences company completed an initial public offering or ceased to be controlled by Canadian private residents, its credit rate immediately dropped to the 15 per cent non-refundable rate. Fourth, the Department of Finance restored capital expenditure eligibility for both the Section 37 deduction against income and the Section 127 investment tax credit components of the SR&ED program. Prior to January 1, 2014, capital expenditures for depreciable property used all or substantially all (90 per cent or more of its operating time over its useful life) for SR&ED in Canada, along with shared-use equipment lease payments, qualified for SR&ED incentives, before being repealed effective January 1, 2014. The restored rules generally match the pre-2014 statutory mechanics and apply to depreciable property acquired on or after the date of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024), and in the case of lease costs, to amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024.
Complementary Federal Tax Incentives: Accelerated CCA and Clean Economy ITCs

In tandem with the SR&ED overhaul, federal tax legislation enacted between 2024 and 2026 introduced complementary capital write-offs and sector-specific investment tax credits that interact directly with corporate R&D capital budgeting. Under Budget 2024, businesses acquiring eligible patents or rights to use patented information, data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software, and general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and system software on or after April 16, 2024, that become available for use before January 1, 2027, qualify for an immediate 100 per cent first-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) deduction. Furthermore, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement proposed reinstating the broader Accelerated Investment Incentive for a five-year window commencing January 1, 2025, for qualifying capital assets becoming available for use before 2030, allowing immediate expensing of capital asset purchases rather than slower annual depreciation. Additionally, to strengthen domestic IP strategy, Budget 2024 committed $14.5 million over two years for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective to assist small and medium-sized enterprises in IP creation and retention, while advancing consultations on a federal patent box regime and amendments to the Red Tape Reduction Act to broaden regulatory sandboxes for temporary product testing.

For industrial innovators operating in energy transition and advanced materials, the federal government also enacted a suite of refundable Clean Economy ITCs—including through Bill C-59—comprising the Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) ITC, the Clean Technology ITC, the Clean Hydrogen ITC, the Clean Electricity ITC, and the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC. Notably, the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC provides a 30 per cent refundable tax credit on the cost of investments in eligible property used all or substantially all for eligible clean technology manufacturing or qualifying mineral activities producing copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium, graphite, and rare earth elements. Recognizing that critical mineral recovery frequently occurs in polymetallic projects, Budget 2024 modified eligible expenditures effective for property acquired on or after January 1, 2024, to include investments at mine or well sites (including tailing ponds, mills, smelters, or refineries) expected to produce primarily—meaning 50 per cent or more of the financial value of the output—qualifying materials, supported by an arm's-length engineer or geoscientist attestation submitted to the CRA and protected against price volatility by a five-year historical average safe harbour rule against ITC recapture. In coordinating these incentives with SR&ED, taxpayers must ensure that the exact same capital asset expenditure is not claimed twice under both a Clean Economy ITC and an SR&ED ITC, and must account for government assistance pool reductions under subsection 127(11.1).

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

Under the statutory mechanics of the ITA, as updated for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6 million Expenditure Limit for a qualifying CCPC or an associated group of qualifying CCPCs is reduced when the group's combined taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15 million. Because the phase-out is linear between $15 million and $75 million (representing a $60 million phase-out span), the expenditure limit is reduced by $10.00 for every $100 of prior-year taxable capital above $15 million:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Eligible Canadian public corporations, and CCPCs that elect under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32), apply the same formula to average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years under subsection 127(10.6).

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, where the legacy $3.0 million limit and $10 million to $50 million taxable capital phase-out apply (representing a $40 million phase-out span), the formula reduces the expenditure limit at a marginal rate of $7.50 for every $100 of prior-year taxable capital above $10 million:

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $10,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000.

While prior to 2019 the federal expenditure limit was also subject to a phase-out based on the preceding year's taxable income, the federal expenditure limit is now phased out solely by reference to taxable capital employed in Canada, although the corporation's qualifying income limit in the preceding taxation year still impacts whether ITCs earned at the general 15 per cent rate on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit qualify for 40 per cent partial refundability. Moreover, certain provincial regimes—most notably Ontario for the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit—continue to enforce a prior-year federal taxable income phase-out between $500,000 and $800,000 alongside a taxable capital phase-out between $25 million and $50 million. Where a corporation has a short taxation year containing fewer than 365 days, the annual expenditure limit must be prorated based on the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
Residency, Territoriality, and the 10 Per Cent Foreign Permissive Rule

A foundational principle of the SR&ED program is territoriality: under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, expenditures must generally be incurred for SR&ED carried on physically inside Canada. For employee payroll expenses, the CRA mandates that the employee be both a tax resident of Canada and physically located in Canada while performing the experimental or directly supporting activities.

The sole statutory exception to physical presence in Canada for current expenditures applies to permissible foreign salaries and wages under the ITA. Under this narrow permissive rule, salaries and wages paid to an employee who is a resident of Canada for SR&ED performed outside Canada may be claimed, provided that the work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer, forms an integral part of an SR&ED project carried on in Canada, and does not exceed 10 per cent of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid by the claimant for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year. Conversely, subcontractor payments for work performed outside Canada never qualify for SR&ED tax incentives; to claim subcontract expenses, the subcontractor must hold a valid Canadian Business Number, GST/HST number, or Social Insurance Number, and all claimed subcontract work must be physically executed within Canada. Consequently, if a claimant engages a Canadian subcontracting company that employs overseas developers or engineers, the claimant is strictly limited to claiming the percentage of the contract work physically completed in Canada.
Salaries, Wages, and the Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada represent the largest expenditure component of the program, generating an effective federal-provincial recovery that can approach 70 per cent of eligible payroll for qualifying CCPCs. Eligible payroll encompasses gross base salary, regular wages, and direct statutory employer contributions to the extent they relate directly to time spent performing SR&ED in Canada.

However, the ITA and Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations enforce stringent anti-avoidance limitations on "specified employees". A specified employee is defined under the Act as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a relative of the controlling shareholder) or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly at any time during the year, 10 per cent or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any related corporation. For specified employees, three interlocking statutory restrictions govern claimable compensation. First, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and stock option benefits are completely disallowed; only regular base salary or wages actually paid qualify. Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the ITA, a specified employee's salary or wages included in SR&ED expenditures is subject to an overall statutory ceiling of 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee. Third, when calculating notional overhead under the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method, Regulation 2900(7) and subsection 2900(8) cap the maximum proxy salary base for each specified employee at the lesser of 75 per cent of total base salary and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year, and mandate that this 2.5 times YMPE ceiling must be shared among associated corporations; the 75 per cent limit applies to the salary base used to compute the PPA, not to the salary of a specified employee directly engaged in SR&ED.
Traditional Method versus Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method

When filing Form T661, a claimant must make an annual election in Part 1—selecting field 160 for the Proxy Method or field 162 for the Traditional Method—to determine how SR&ED overhead and supporting expenditures are calculated. Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the choice between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method is irrevocable for that year.

body.text: Materials Consumed, Materials Transformed, and Subcontractor Rules

Under Form T661 Part 3, claimants may include the cost of materials used in Canada before the end of the taxation year, categorized into materials consumed and materials transformed. Materials consumed encompass physical substances that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during the experimental process, such as chemical reagents, cell cultures, and assay kits in biotechnology trials, or scrap materials destroyed during prototype testing. Materials transformed comprise physical materials integrated into prototypes, pilot plants, or experimental devices during the SR&ED investigation. Where materials transformed or SR&ED capital properties are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules in Section 127 of the ITA (alongside parallel provincial recapture rules in Alberta and Ontario for the ORDTC) are triggered, adding back the recaptured credit to federal or provincial tax otherwise payable in the year of disposition or commercial conversion.

Payments to external entities for SR&ED performed in Canada are governed by strict statutory reductions and relational distinctions across Form T661. Where a claimant contracts with an arm's length Canadian subcontractor to perform SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100 per cent of the eligible contract expense is deductible in the Section 37 pool, but only 80 per cent of the eligible contract payment may be included in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool to earn ITCs, resulting in an effective federal-provincial credit recovery of approximately 30 per cent of subcontract costs for a qualifying CCPC. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or research consortia must be reported on a separate Form T661 Schedule A (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each third-party payment and are subject to the 80 per cent inclusion rule for federal ITC purposes. Conversely, non-arm's length transactions must be reported on Form T661 Schedule C (Non-Arm's Length Transactions), as payments made to a non-arm's length subcontractor do not qualify for ITCs in the hands of the payer.
Cloud Computing, Software Licenses, and AI Infrastructure

As software development, artificial intelligence, and computational life sciences increasingly rely on on-demand cloud computing arrangements (delivering software, servers, data storage, and networking infrastructure over the internet or private networks via Software-as-a-Service, Platform-as-a-Service, or Infrastructure-as-a-Service models), the treatment of cloud and software costs has become a major focal point of accounting standards and CRA audit reviews. Under Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE), entities entering cloud computing arrangements frequently obtain only a contractual right to access the vendor's software rather than control over a tangible or intangible asset, causing implementation and subscription expenditures to be expensed.

For SR&ED tax purposes, however, financial statement expensing does not automatically confer tax credit eligibility. Under current CRA administrative policy, cloud computing charges (such as AWS compute fees) and software license fees are not claimable as direct SR&ED expenditures for software and IT claimants electing the Proxy Method, because they are neither direct salaries, subcontractors, nor physical materials consumed or transformed, and any utility or facility overhead element is deemed already compensated through the 55 per cent Prescribed Proxy Amount. Only where a taxpayer elects the Traditional Method and maintains granular cost-allocation records proving that dedicated cloud computing and AI research infrastructure costs are wholly incremental and directly attributable to experimental trials—and completely segregated from commercial hosting or routine pre-trained model usage—can such infrastructure costs be considered within traditional overhead. To address the massive capital cost of AI compute outside the constraints of the SR&ED proxy formula, the federal government proposed $2.4 billion in AI sector investments in Budget 2024, anchored by $2.0 billion for an AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million to accelerate AI adoption and startup commercialization, and $100 million for the National Research Council's AI Assist Program to help Canadian SMEs build and deploy AI solutions.
Unpaid Amounts (Subsection 127(26)) and Government Assistance Stacking

Taxpayers must carefully reconcile accrual accounting with the cash-payment gates of the ITA and government assistance pool reductions. Under Form T661 Schedule B (Special Situations) Section 2 (line 552) and Part 3 Step 3 (line 315), unpaid amounts—other than salaries or wages, which are governed by parallel 180-day payment rules—that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which they were incurred are deemed under subsection 127(26) of the ITA not to have been incurred in that year for ITC purposes, and can only be added to the qualified expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.

Furthermore, both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance or non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED. Government assistance encompasses direct federal and provincial innovation grants—such as NRC IRAP contributions, Strategic Innovation Fund disbursements, and CanExport Innovation grants—as well as provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC, OBRITC, and ORDTC, or the Alberta IEG). Conversely, when a taxpayer repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the deductible or qualified SR&ED expenditure pool, the repayment is added back to the Section 37 pool on Form T661 Schedule B Section 1 (line 454) and to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool in Part 3 Step 3 (lines 559 and 560) in the year the repayment is made.
Illustrative Combined Federal-Provincial Stacking Calculation (Ontario CCPC)

To demonstrate the mathematical interaction between the Prescribed Proxy Amount, provincial R&D tax credits, government assistance pool reductions, and the federal SR&ED ITC, consider a qualifying CCPC with a permanent establishment in Ontario during a taxation year governed by the post-December 16, 2024 reformed regime. Assume the corporation incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries in Ontario, elects the Proxy Method, has prior-year taxable capital below $15 million and prior-year federal taxable income below $500,000, and claims both the refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC at 8 per cent) and the non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC at 3.5 per cent) without waiving either credit.

Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly every Canadian province and the Yukon territory supplement the federal SR&ED program with regional R&D tax incentives. With the exception of Québec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits piggyback directly on the federal SR&ED definition under subsection 248(1) of the ITA and are administered by the CRA through provincial schedules attached to the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Jurisdictions
Ontario's Three-Tiered Architecture and Capital Restoration Alignment

Ontario operates a stratified R&D tax ecosystem harmonized with the federal CRA administration since January 1, 2009. Small and medium-sized corporations benefit primarily from the 8 per cent refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, claimed on Schedule 566) on up to $3 million of qualified expenditures (yielding up to $240,000 annually in cash refunds), alongside the 3.5 per cent non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, claimed on Schedule 508) and the 20 per cent refundable Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, capped at $20 million in annual qualified expenditures). Crucially, following the December 2024 federal Fall Economic Statement, the Ontario government updated the statutory parameters of the OITC to confirm that an Ontario qualified expenditure includes 100 per cent of current expenditures, 40 per cent of qualified capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014, zero per cent of capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, and 100 per cent of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024. Because the OITC, OBRITC, and ORDTC all reduce the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures, Ontario explicitly permits corporations to waive the OITC or ORDTC in whole or in part by filing a written waiver with their T2 return within six months of their taxation year-end or on an amended return for that year. Beyond R&D credits, Ontario industrial and technology firms frequently pair SR&ED with the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit (providing a 15 per cent credit on up to $3 million per year in eligible buildings and production machinery through December 31, 2029, refundable for CCPCs and non-refundable for non-CCPCs) and the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (offering a 35 per cent to 40 per cent refundable credit on eligible Ontario labour certified by Ontario Creates within 18 months of year-end).
Québec's Independent Administration and the March 25, 2025 Structural Overhaul

Unlike the rest of Canada, Québec administers its corporate tax and R&D incentive regime autonomously through Revenu Québec. Historically, corporations and qualified partnerships carrying out R&D in Québec claimed incentives across a fragmented suite of specific refundable credits: the Tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7, with associated corporation expenditure limit allocations on Form RD-1029.7.8), the Tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03), and the Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), where enhanced rates applied to an expenditure limit of $3 million.

However, in its March 25, 2025 budget measures, Québec enacted a decisive legislative consolidation of its R&D tax architecture. Specifically, for any fiscal period beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated five legacy tax credits: the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and the tax credit for technological adaptation services (as well as industrial design tax credits). In their place, for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Revenu Québec established a unified tax credit framework, the tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization (CRIC), covering both R&D and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec by or on behalf of a qualified corporation or partnership. Under this reformed post-March 25, 2025 Québec regime, qualifying expenditures encompass four distinct categories: salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to certain research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property. Tax practitioners and corporate controllers auditing Québec operations across 2025 and 2026 must strictly bifurcate fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, from those beginning after March 25, 2025, while noting that Revenu Québec also transitioned to mandatory online business communications starting in fall 2025.
Alberta's Incremental Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Following the expiration of the legacy 10 per cent Alberta SR&ED tax credit for expenditures incurred before January 1, 2020, Alberta introduced the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) for eligible expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Administered via Alberta Schedule 29 and guided by Alberta Corporate Income Tax Information Circular IEG-1, the IEG provides benefits on up to $4 million in annual Alberta R&D spending that matches federal SR&ED eligibility rules. The grant is structured as a two-tier incremental calculation: qualified corporations receive an 8 per cent payment for eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated from the preceding two years' average spending), and an enhanced 20 per cent payment for eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level. Eligible expenditures for the IEG must be reduced by government and non-government assistance other than the Alberta credit and the federal SR&ED ITC, and any IEG received reduces the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures. Unlike the 18-month federal filing deadline, the statutory deadline for claiming the Alberta IEG is 15 months after the corporation's Alberta filing due date (i.e., 21 months after fiscal year-end).
Competitive Advantage for Large Corporations in Manitoba and Atlantic Canada

A critical strategic divergence emerges when evaluating provincial regimes for large corporations—specifically those exceeding $50 million to $75 million in taxable capital or foreign-controlled multinational subsidiaries. In Ontario, a large corporation is completely phased out of the 8 per cent refundable OITC once prior-year taxable capital reaches $50 million (or prior-year taxable income reaches $800,000), leaving it eligible solely for the 3.5 per cent non-refundable ORDTC alongside the 15 per cent non-refundable federal ITC (a combined rate of approximately 18.5 per cent before assistance adjustments). By contrast, Manitoba and the Maritime/Atlantic provinces (such as New Brunswick and Newfoundland and Labrador) offer large firms 15 per cent provincial R&D tax credits with no expenditure caps and no taxable capital phase-outs. In New Brunswick and Newfoundland and Labrador, the entire 15 per cent credit is fully refundable, while in Manitoba, the 15 per cent credit is 50 per cent refundable (7.5 per cent refundable and 7.5 per cent non-refundable) for in-house R&D and 100 per cent refundable (15 per cent) when conducted under contract with a qualifying educational institution. Consequently, large corporations locating R&D centres in Manitoba or Atlantic Canada earn nearly double the combined R&D tax credit rate of an equivalent large corporation in Ontario (30 per cent nominal combined rate versus 18.5 per cent).
Governing Bodies, Filing Procedures, and Statutory Deadlines
Institutional Architecture and Review Streams

The administration of R&D tax incentives and complementary innovation grants in Canada involves a clear division of responsibilities across federal and provincial agencies. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) holds exclusive statutory authority to assess and audit federal SR&ED claims as well as harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits outside Québec and Alberta. Within the CRA, technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the ITA is evaluated by specialized Research and Technology Advisors, while accounting ledgers, payroll summaries, subcontractor eligibility, and government assistance deductions are verified by financial auditors.

Alongside the tax administration of the CRA, non-tax direct federal R&D funding is delivered primarily by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) through the Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—which provides direct financial contributions to Canadian SMEs alongside specialized sub-streams including AI Assist, IP Assist, Youth Employment, and Clean Technology—as well as Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) through the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), the $2 billion Global Innovation Clusters, CanExport Innovation (providing direct-to-recipient R&D export grants), and regional development agencies such as FedDev Ontario (Business Scale-up and Productivity) and the Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation (NOHFC). Because all direct grants and non-repayable contributions from NRC IRAP, SIF, and regional agencies constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, recipients must deduct those grant amounts from their qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661.
Mandatory Tax Forms and Prescribed Information

To submit a valid federal SR&ED claim, a taxpayer must file a complete set of prescribed forms with the CRA. Every claimant carrying out SR&ED in Canada must complete Form T661 (Claim for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Carried Out in Canada), guided by CRA Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661). Where a claimant is a partner in a partnership that incurred SR&ED expenditures, a separate Form T661 must be filed to support the SR&ED expenditures incurred by each partnership.
Form T661 is organized into sequential parts and mandatory schedules that must be completed accurately for the claim to be accepted as prescribed information:

headers: Core Statutory Function and Required Disclosures

cells: Captures claimant identification, business number, and the mandatory election of the expenditure reporting method in Field 160 (Proxy Method) or Field 162 (Traditional Method), plus the signed Certification and Election section.

Requires project-by-project technical descriptions demonstrating how the work meets SR&ED eligibility requirements (technological uncertainties, systematic experimental investigation, and technological advancements), along with the distribution of effort between Basic research (Line 650), Applied research (Line 652), and Experimental development, and retention of supporting contemporaneous evidence.
Form T661 — Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures)

Step 1 breaks down allowable SR&ED expenditures (including salaries, materials consumed/transformed, subcontractors, and lease costs where 50% of primarily used equipment lease costs are entered under the proxy method and "0" under the traditional method); Step 2 calculates the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under s. 37(1) (incorporating Line 454 adjustments); and Step 3 computes qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 380, 390, 557–560), adjusting for unpaid amounts under subsection 127(26) (Line 315 / Line 552) and repayments of assistance.
Reports statistical and background classification data regarding the nature and personnel of the SR&ED claim.
Third-Party Payments for SR&ED — A separate Schedule A must be completed and attached to Form T661 for each third-party payment for SR&ED.

Special Situations — Section 1 computes adjustments to the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada (including repayments of government and non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool, reported on Line 454); Section 2 computes adjustments to qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes, including unpaid amounts deemed not incurred in the year under subsection 127(26) (reported on Lines 552 and 554).
Non-Arm's Length Transactions — Tracks current expenditures and adjustments arising from non-arm's length SR&ED transactions.
Form T661 — Schedules D, E, and F
Supplemental schedules attached to Form T661 where applicable, including allocation of the specified employee 2.5× YMPE proxy salary base across associated corporations under Regulation 2900(8).

Investment Tax Credit – Corporations (Schedule 31) or Investment Tax Credit (Individuals) (Form T2038(IND)) — Must be filed alongside Form T661 to identify capital and current expenditures qualifying for an ITC, calculate the 15% or 35% credit, allocate the expenditure limit among associated corporations, and claim refunds or carryforwards.

body.text: The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Zero Fairness Discretion

One of the most unforgiving procedural traps in Canadian tax law is the SR&ED reporting deadline governed by subsection 37(11) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Under these provisions, expenditures for SR&ED qualifying for a deduction or an ITC must be identified by the claimant on a completed Form T661 and Schedule 31 (or Form T2038(IND)) no later than 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is six months after the end of its taxation year, adding the 12-month reporting period establishes an absolute statutory deadline of 18 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year. If a claimant files an initial Form T661 on time but forgets to claim a specific expenditure, the claimant has up to that same 12-month post-filing-due-date cutoff (18 months after corporate fiscal year-end) to submit an amended Form T661.

Crucially, the Income Tax Act does not permit late-filed Form T661 or Schedule 31 forms. If a corporation fails to file Form T661 and Schedule 31—or fails to identify a specific expenditure on those prescribed forms—by the 18-month deadline, the expenditure is permanently barred from SR&ED treatment, and the CRA possesses zero statutory or administrative "fairness" discretion to accept a late-filed claim.
Judicial Precedents, Case Law, and CRA Audit Enforcement

Because subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines SR&ED in broad conceptual terms rather than rigid industry checklists, Canadian tax courts have established the definitive legal framework for technical eligibility. Every CRA Research and Technology Advisor review and every Tax Court of Canada appeal is governed by binding jurisprudence anchored by Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen.
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998, Tax Court of Canada), the Court established the five foundational criteria for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under the ITA, a test subsequently affirmed and adopted as binding appellate law by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (following the Tax Court of Canada decision in August 2000) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88. To qualify as SR&ED under the Northwest Hydraulic framework, a claimant's project must satisfy five cumulative criteria:

First, the court examines whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. For a project to qualify as SR&ED-eligible, the taxpayer must have faced the risk that the technical objective could not be achieved satisfactorily due to genuine technological obstacles or unknowns, rather than routine engineering, standard configuration, quality control, or commercial/market uncertainty. Second, the inquiry asks whether the person claiming to be performing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis, rather than unguided trial-and-error tinkering. Fourth, the process must be undertaken for the purpose of resulting in a technological advancement—meaning an advancement in the state of technological knowledge, including conclusive findings from failed experimental iterations that prove a hypothesized approach cannot succeed. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the experimental results must be maintained as the work progresses.
Appellate Reaffirmation of the Scientific Method: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88)

For years, a recurring point of contention in SR&ED tax litigation involved taxpayers arguing that the "scientific method" and formal "hypothesis" requirements articulated in Northwest Hydraulic did not appear anywhere in the statutory text of Canada's Income Tax Act and therefore should not be enforced as strict legal prerequisites. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (decided in May 2021), the Federal Court of Appeal decisively rejected this argument and reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic criteria as mandatory law.

In Kam-Press, the taxpayer argued that because the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act contains no literal reference to the "scientific method," the Tax Court of Canada erred by applying that criterion to disallow its manufacturing development claim. The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria had been consistently adopted by prior appellate decisions of the Court (including C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada) as the proper legal interpretation of a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Following Kam-Press, claimants across all industrial, manufacturing, biotechnology, and software sectors are legally required to demonstrate adherence to the scientific method—specifically linking technological uncertainties to formulated hypotheses and systematic experimental testing.
Evidentiary Standards, Contemporaneous Documentation, and Sectoral Audit Trends (2024–2026)

In recent enforcement cycles through 2025 and 2026, the CRA has instituted stricter interpretations of "systematic investigation" and heightened contemporaneous documentation requirements across high-claim sectors, particularly biotechnology, life sciences, artificial intelligence, and software consulting. Rather than accepting retrospective post-project summaries drafted at year-end, the CRA increasingly requires real-time experimental records generated as the work happens, such as digital laboratory notebooks, specialized R&D tracking logs, detailed records of failed experiments and failed model versions, and direct correlations linking research staff wages and AI-generated data analytics to specific experimental hypotheses and project milestones.

In the biotechnology and life sciences sector, CRA audit guidelines draw a sharp boundary between eligible scientific experimentation and ineligible regulatory compliance. Phase II clinical trial expenses, drug formulation optimization, and prototype or pilot plant costs in biologics manufacturing qualify for SR&ED when they are designed to resolve unknown therapeutic outcomes or defined scientific uncertainties. Conversely, routine stability testing and expenses incurred purely for Health Canada regulatory approval—such as Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance testing—do not qualify unless tied directly to resolving an underlying scientific uncertainty Budget 2026, tabled on November 5, 2026, proposes to extend SR&ED eligibility, for taxation years beginning on or after that date, to tests, technological validations and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for the initial approval or certification needed to commercialize a product or process, where those activities directly relate to an eligible SR&ED project, and to the costs of registering and maintaining patents and other intellectual property protection for intellectual property developed in an eligible SR&ED project.. Similarly, where artificial intelligence and machine learning are integrated into life sciences or software R&D, the CRA distinguishes between experimental AI models trained on new data to resolve algorithmic uncertainties (such as whether a novel algorithm can predict molecular binding affinity), which are eligible, and the routine use or deployment of pre-trained AI models, which is ineligible.

In the software and IT consulting sector, CRA audit scrutiny focuses heavily on separating technological uncertainty from routine software development and verifying contractual entitlement when work is performed for paying clients. While a widespread misconception suggests that software consultants cannot claim SR&ED if they are paid by a client for their work, eligibility actually turns on whether the client is a Canadian taxpayer claiming SR&ED on that same project. If a Canadian client claims SR&ED for the contracted work, the software consultant is barred from claiming SR&ED on the same work; however, if the project was completed for a company that does not claim SR&ED—and particularly where the work was performed for a foreign client, since no foreign client can claim Canadian SR&ED—the Canadian software consultant can generally claim the eligible Canadian R&D payroll directly.
Strategic Synthesis and Audit Readiness Recommendations

Navigating Canada's modernized R&D tax architecture requires synchronizing corporate tax planning, cost accounting, and real-time engineering documentation. First, corporations with taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, should immediately reconfigure their capital asset and lease tracking ledgers to capture restored SR&ED capital expenditures and shared-use equipment lease payments, while mid-market CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital between $10 million and $75 million, and eligible Canadian public corporations, should model their expanded entitlement under the $6 million expenditure limit and the $2.1 million refundable federal ITC ceiling (alongside Ontario's parallel restoration of 100 per cent capital expenditure eligibility under the OITC effective December 16, 2024). Second, enterprises operating establishments or partnerships in Québec must transition their tax compliance workflows away from the five eliminated legacy Revenu Québec R&D credits for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, ensuring that R&D and pre-commercialization salaries, subcontractor payments, research organization payments, and capital property acquisitions are captured under the consolidated post-March 25, 2025 Québec framework.

Third, founder-led corporations must structure executive researcher remuneration as regular payroll salary rather than bonuses or dividends to comply with the specified employee rules, apply the 75 per cent and 2.5 times YMPE proxy salary base caps (and share the cap across associated corporations on Regulation 2900(8) schedules), verify that all non-salary SR&ED accruals are paid within 180 days of year-end under subsection 127(26), and evaluate whether waiving non-refundable provincial credits such as the 3.5 per cent Ontario ORDTC within six months of year-end yields a higher net cash refund through the 35 per cent federal ITC pool. Finally, to safeguard claims against CRA technical review and satisfy the binding appellate standard of Northwest Hydraulic and Kam-Press Metal Products, organizations must institutionalize contemporaneous documentation—recording explicit hypotheses, experimental test protocols, quantitative test results, and failed iterations in real time as the research progresses—while enforcing internal filing controls well ahead of the absolute 18-month statutory deadline under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act.
